notes_markdown:
### Changed

- **empty book folders are now created only if you ask for them**, matching how
  Sonarr works. Settings > Media Management > **Create Empty Book Folders**,
  off by default. It covers all three places a folder gets made: adding a book,
  changing its root folder, and a disk scan. As in Sonarr, turning on "delete
  empty folders" suppresses it — creating a folder something else is set to
  sweep away only churns it.

  **If you had previously saved the Media Management page, your existing
  behaviour is preserved and the new setting comes up on.** A fresh install, or
  one that never saved that page, will have it off.

### Fixed

- a file's folder and its name are stored in separate places, and one importer
  was writing the whole file path into the folder column. Anything that later
  looked for that file built a path that could not exist, so a refresh treated
  it as missing and dropped the record. Fixed, and a repair pass runs once at
  startup to correct any record already written that way — it reports what it
  changed on the Tasks page and does nothing at all when there is nothing wrong.

- re-importing the same download created a second, duplicate record of every
  file, because the check for "do I already have this?" compared a full file
  path against a column holding folders and so never matched.

- an upgrade whose new file landed at exactly the same path as the one it
  replaced could leave the book with no file records at all, and could keep
  re-running the same upgrade indefinitely because the record still described
  the old file's audio.

- moving a book kept its files' sub-folders (`Disc 1`, `CD2`) in one place and
  flattened them in three others, so after some moves those files could no
  longer be found. All four now behave the same way.

- if a move succeeded on disk but the database write that followed it failed,
  the folder stayed at its new location while ABM still pointed at the old one.
  The folder is now put back.

- bulk edits that move books now save each book as it goes, so one failure part
  way through no longer leaves every folder already moved unaccounted for.

- the root folder removal dialog described two things that do not happen: that
  removing a folder leaves everything else untouched, and that deleting its
  files also deletes the books. It now says what actually happens, and the book
  count it shows is correct — a root folder whose name began with another one's
  name was counting the other folder's books as its own.

- a scan skipped reconciling any book whose folder was missing, so a book whose
  files had gone was never noticed.

- a converted book kept reporting the quality it had before conversion. The
  conversion refreshed the file's format but left the audio properties read from
  the original, and the quality classifier trusts those over the extension — so
  an upgraded-by-conversion book could look like it still needed upgrading.

- a background task that failed while saving recorded its own failure against a
  session that first needed resetting, so the failure could go unrecorded.

- the startup file-path repair was registered as safe to retry after a database
  lock but could never actually retry, because it reported the lock as a result
  rather than raising it.

### Fixed

- moving books to a different root folder reported success while moving
  nothing. Every book was sent with the same hardcoded source path, taken from
  a field the server has never returned, so the move either failed outright or
  skipped every book — and the result was reported as "Successfully moved N
  books" regardless, because the response was never read. Each book's source is
  now worked out from where that book actually is, so a selection spanning
  several root folders moves correctly in one go, and the result now says how
  many books moved and why any were left behind.

- moving a book whose files sit in sub-folders (`Disc 1`, `CD2`) rewrote every
  file's recorded location to the book folder itself, so those files could no
  longer be found after the move. Sub-folders are now preserved.

- a book added to a root folder other than the default recorded that choice but
  had nowhere to record where its folder would be, unless the folder happened to
  be created at the same moment. A book's destination is now always recorded
  when it is added, and creating the folder on disk is a separate step — the
  same split Sonarr uses. **Adding a book now requires at least one root folder
  to be configured**, and says so plainly rather than creating a book with no
  destination.

- the root folder list counted every book whose path merely began with the same
  characters, so a root folder named as a prefix of another reported the other
  one's books as its own — including in the confirmation shown before removing
  a root folder. Counts are now bounded at a folder boundary.

### Fixed

- adding a book to a root folder other than the default recorded that choice
  but built the book's folder under the **default** root anyway, so the book's
  recorded location and its actual location disagreed from the moment it was
  created. The folder is now built under the root folder that was actually
  chosen.

### Fixed

- a library scan or a book's refresh read an unreachable library folder as the
  book's files having been deleted. It removed every tracked `File` row for
  that book and marked it `wanted` — which is what tells Audiobook Manager to
  go re-acquire it from indexers. A dropped network mount (NFS, SMB) presents
  on disk exactly like a folder someone emptied or deleted, and nothing
  distinguished the two, so an outage during a scan could wipe file records and
  queue an entire library for re-download.

  A book is now judged against the root folder it actually lives under rather
  than whichever root the scan happened to be walking, which is what made this
  worse the more root folders you had. A root that is missing is never trusted.
  A root that is merely empty only blocks the destructive path when that book
  already has tracked files — so a brand-new, empty root folder can still have
  its first folder created on it without being mistaken for an outage. A root
  that cannot be listed at all (a stale mount handle, an I/O error) is now
  treated as missing rather than healthy, which is the most common way a
  failing mount actually behaves.

  The same false reading reached three further places, all now fixed: applying
  fetched metadata set a book to `wanted` on an unreachable path before the
  scan's own check ever ran; refreshing a book reported "Refreshed book" on
  success when nothing had been touched; and a batch refresh counted every
  skipped book as a successful one.

- **a scan no longer creates a missing library root folder.** It used to create
  the folder and carry on, which is the same blind spot — an unmounted share is
  indistinguishable from a folder that was never made, and creating it destroys
  the evidence that anything was wrong. A missing root now stops the scan
  instead. If you relied on a scan to create your library folder, create it
  yourself first; adding a root folder already required the path to exist, so
  this only affects a scan against a root whose folder later went missing.

- the Health page reported root folders as accessible when a mount had dropped.
  It only checked whether the folder existed, so an empty mountpoint — the
  usual symptom — read as healthy. It now reports an empty root that still has
  books recorded under it as an error, while a new root folder with nothing in
  it yet stays healthy.

  A scan that skips books now says so on the Tasks page, rather than reporting
  no changes.

  Not covered: a mount that fails *below* a configured root folder — where the
  root itself is local and an inner folder is the mount point — still looks
  healthy from the root, and is handled as before.

### Fixed

- `0.15.1` got the ownership model backwards. It made an Audiobookshelf edit
  the way to opt a book out: ABM saw a `metadata.json` with no `"abm"` block
  and left that book alone from then on. That hands the source of truth to
  Audiobookshelf for any book you touch there, which is the opposite of what
  ABM is for. ABM now writes its own value and re-stamps the `"abm"` block
  every time, for any book in its catalogue, whatever the file contained
  before. The block is a provenance stamp, not a permission gate — ownership
  is decided by the book being in ABM's library, not by what is in the file.

  **If you edited a book's metadata in Audiobookshelf while `0.15.1` was
  running:** ABM stopped managing that book and will now resume. Your
  Audiobookshelf edit will be replaced with ABM's value on that book's next
  add, import, or refresh. There is no per-book opt-out yet; if you need one
  for a particular book, keep it out of ABM's library for now.

- a book correctly filed under a real, configured root folder that was not
  the default — and whose `root_folder_id` was never set to it — was refused
  by its directory listing, a manual import's conflict check, a manual import
  itself, and creating any of `cover.jpg`, `reader.txt`, `desc.txt`, or
  `title.opf`. Each of those resolved a single library path (the book's
  assigned root folder, or the default one) before ever looking at where the
  book's folder actually was, so a book filed correctly anywhere else came
  back "No root folder configured" while its files sat right there.

  Those seven checks now share one lookup that asks where the book's folder
  actually is before asking which root folder it was assigned to. A root
  folder is still required to work out where a book *should* go; it is no
  longer consulted to find a folder that already exists.

### Fixed

- the `metadata.json` ownership marker `0.15.0` shipped as a separate
  hidden `.abm.json` file inverted the behavior that marker was supposed to
  produce. Audiobookshelf never reads or writes `.abm.json`, so ABM
  believed it owned `metadata.json` forever regardless of what happened to
  it — meaning an edit made directly inside Audiobookshelf would be
  silently reverted the next time ABM touched the book, exactly backwards
  from the `0.15.0` entry below's claim that editing in Audiobookshelf was
  how you'd opt a book out. The marker is now an `"abm"` block written
  inside `metadata.json` itself. Audiobookshelf ignores that block on read
  and always discards it on its own rewrite, so editing a book's metadata
  in Audiobookshelf is now what tells ABM to back off: ABM sees a
  `metadata.json` with no block and leaves it alone from then on. Deleting
  the block by hand does the same thing. `.abm.json` is no longer read or
  written at all.

  **If ABM wrote a book's `metadata.json` while `0.15.0` was running:**
  that file has no `"abm"` block, so as of this release ABM treats it as
  foreign and will not touch it again on its own. If you want ABM to keep
  managing that book, delete its `metadata.json` (and the now-unused
  `.abm.json` beside it, if present) — the next import or refresh
  regenerates it correctly. If you're fine with what `0.15.0` wrote and
  don't want it changed, no action is needed; that's now the same outcome
  as having edited it in Audiobookshelf.

### Added

- ABM now writes Audiobookshelf's own `metadata.json` into every book's
  folder — the file at the very top of Audiobookshelf's metadata
  precedence, above everything else ABM has ever contributed (embedded
  tags, `.opf`, `reader.txt`, even the folder name itself). Title,
  subtitle, authors, narrators, series, genres, publication year and date,
  publisher, description, ASIN, and language go in using Audiobookshelf's
  own schema, with author and narrator names written verbatim — this is the
  one channel that doesn't have to mangle a name to dodge Audiobookshelf's
  own splitting rules the way tags and `reader.txt` do. A hidden
  `.abm.json` marker sits beside it so ABM can tell its own file apart from
  one Audiobookshelf wrote or a user edited by hand: a later refresh only
  overwrites `metadata.json` when that marker is present, and leaves a
  foreign one alone.

  **`metadata.json` always writes on add, import, and refresh — none of the
  four "Create metadata files" toggles or three trigger settings in
  Settings > Metadata govern it, and there is currently no way to turn it
  off.** If you edit a book's metadata directly inside Audiobookshelf, that
  edit will be overwritten the next time ABM touches the book, because
  `metadata.json` now outranks it. If you don't want ABM controlling a
  particular book's metadata this way, delete `.abm.json` from its folder —
  ABM treats a folder without that marker as foreign from then on.

### Fixed

- `cover.jpg`, `title.opf`, `desc.txt`, and `reader.txt` were never created
  for a book acquired the normal way — indexer search, grab, download
  client, import — no matter what Settings > Metadata said. The handler for
  that path never called the metadata service at all, so none of the four
  file toggles and none of the three trigger settings had any effect on it;
  only a manual "Create" button or a library-import run ever produced these
  files. It's now wired into both a fresh import and a quality-upgrade
  replace, running after the transaction is committed and isolated from the
  import itself — a sidecar failure can never fail the import. **If you've
  had these settings enabled and wondered why your books never got a
  cover.jpg or reader.txt:** this is why. They'll start appearing on the
  next import; existing books pick them up on their next refresh or a
  manual "Create" action.
- the sidecar writer stopped creating a book's folder as a side effect of
  writing files into it. Harmless on its own before this release, since the
  only caller that could reach it with a missing folder was gated off — but
  now that sidecar generation runs on every import, an unconditional
  `mkdir` here would have quietly defeated the "Skip Folder Creation"
  library setting. It now skips with a logged reason when the folder
  doesn't exist instead of creating it.
- sidecar files (cover, OPF, desc, reader.txt, and now `metadata.json`)
  silently failed to write for a book sitting in a perfectly valid on-disk
  folder whenever no default root folder was configured. The folder lookup
  resolved a library root before ever checking whether the book already had
  a folder on disk, so the one case that doesn't need a root folder at all
  still needed one — and hit it. Fixed: the on-disk path is checked first.
- a book's `.opf` file and its embedded audio tags have always produced a
  malformed genre entry for any book with more than one genre.
  `Book.genres` is stored as one comma-joined string, but both the OPF
  writer's `<dc:subject>` loop and the audio-tag writer's `TCON` field
  wrapped that whole string in a single-item list instead of splitting it —
  so "Fantasy, Adventure" came out as one `<dc:subject>Fantasy,
  Adventure</dc:subject>` tag instead of two, and as a comma-separated
  `TCON` value instead of the slash-separated one Audiobookshelf's tag
  reader expects. Both now split the column correctly. **This doesn't
  rewrite what's already on disk** — an already-written `.opf` or a file
  that's already been tagged still carries the malformed genre value;
  regenerate the OPF or re-tag the file to pick up the fix.

### Fixed

- author and narrator names written to tags, `reader.txt`, and `.opf` files
  could still be split apart by Audiobookshelf after `0.14.3`'s fix for
  exactly that problem — `0.14.3` sanitized a name by replacing `&` with
  the literal word `" and "`, but `" and "` is Audiobookshelf's own second
  split, right behind `&`. With two or more names the join's own `&`
  still won and covered for it, but most books have only one name — with
  nothing to join, there was no `&` at all, so Audiobookshelf split on the
  `" and "` the sanitizer had just inserted. `Anne & Todd McCaffrey` came
  out of `0.14.3` as two authors, `Anne` and `Todd McCaffrey`. A name that
  legitimately contains the word "and" (`Crosby and Nash`) split the same
  way. Both are fixed the same way now: `&`, `,`, `;`, and the literal
  word `" and "` are all stripped out of a name before joining, so nothing
  Audiobookshelf treats as a separator is left inside a single name.
  **If a name in your library contains `&` or the word "and":** that text
  is now dropped from what ABM writes for it — `Anne & Todd McCaffrey` is
  written as `Anne Todd McCaffrey` — because leaving any of it in is what
  caused the split. This doesn't rewrite what's already on disk; re-tag a
  book or regenerate its `reader.txt` / `.opf` to pick up the corrected
  name.
- adding chapters to a book in place — Chapterize, and the in-place case of
  `0.14.3`'s hardlink-safety fix — staged its temp file next to the real
  file with a real audio extension and no protection against a same-named
  collision. A library scan or the file watcher could see the half-written,
  multi-gigabyte remux mid-write and treat it as a new audio file; and
  because the file's own name carried nothing more than a process ID, two
  chapter operations landing on same-extension files in the same folder at
  the same moment could stage to the identical path and race each other's
  swap onto the live file. Staging now uses a collision-proof name that
  scans and the file watcher never mistake for real content, with ffmpeg
  told the container explicitly since the staged name no longer carries a
  usable extension. The swap also now carries the original file's
  permissions across, which it didn't before — the staged file was created
  more restrictively than the original, so a completed chapter add could
  quietly leave a file only ABM's own user could read.
- the hardlink-safety fix in `0.14.3` (copying a file to a private inode
  before an in-place tag or cover write) could leave a permanent orphan
  file behind in the library folder if ABM was interrupted between staging
  the copy and swapping it in — its temp file had no suffix a cleanup pass
  could recognize, so nothing ever came back for it. It now stages through
  the same collision-proof, sweepable temp file as the chapter fix above,
  and a leftover from an earlier interruption is cleaned up automatically
  the next time the same operation runs on that folder.

  **If you already have a stray file from a crash before this fix:** the
  automatic sweep only recognizes the new naming pattern. Look for a dotfile
  next to a book's audio file that isn't `cover.jpg`, `reader.txt`, or
  `.opf` — for chapters, named like `.temp_chapters_<pid>_<time>.m4b` or
  `.chapters_temp_<pid>.m4b`; for a tag or cover write, named like
  `.<book file>.<random>` with no extension at all. Safe to delete by hand;
  nothing in ABM will pick it back up.

### Fixed

- writing a tag or embedding cover art into a book file that's still
  hardlinked to a seeding torrent edited the seeding copy in place — ABM and
  the torrent client shared the same inode, since hardlinking is the default
  behavior when `useHardlinks` is on, and mutagen writes to a hardlinked file
  in place. The first tag write or cover embed after import could break that
  torrent's hash check. ABM now checks for a shared link before writing and,
  if one exists, copies the file to a private one in the same directory
  first, so the seeding copy is never touched. **This only protects writes
  going forward.** If you've been running with hardlinks on, any torrent
  whose book got tagged or had a cover embedded after import may already
  have a broken hash — check your client for anything that's stopped
  seeding or failed its recheck, and re-add it if so.
- adding chapters to a book in place could damage a seeding torrent the same
  way, by a different route. The chaptered file was written to the system temp
  directory and then moved onto the library file — and when those sit on
  different filesystems, as they do in any normal Docker setup, that move
  becomes a copy that rewrites the existing file's contents rather than
  replacing it, so the seeding copy's bytes changed underneath it. The
  chaptered file is now written alongside the book and swapped in by renaming,
  so the seeding copy keeps exactly the bytes it was hashed against. The same
  caveat applies — this protects writes going forward, not ones already made.
- creating `cover.jpg` for a book with a custom cover failed with "Cover URL
  rejected: URL scheme '' not allowed". A custom cover is stored inside ABM and
  referenced by an internal path rather than a web address, so the download
  step rejected it. It now copies the stored custom cover into the book folder
  instead — which matters when the folder's `cover.jpg` has been deleted or the
  book has been reorganised, since that button is how you'd put it back.
- a book's `.opf` metadata file came out with malformed XML if its title,
  author, narrator, publisher, ASIN, genre, language, or series name
  contained `&`, `<`, or `>` — only the description was ever escaped.
  Audiobookshelf discards a `.opf` it can't parse, silently, so any affected
  book's OPF was never actually read. Every field is escaped now, and the
  series name and position are quoted properly. **If you've generated an
  OPF for a book whose metadata contains one of those characters:**
  regenerate it — this fix doesn't rewrite files already on disk.
- `reader.txt` listed narrators one per line, but Audiobookshelf only reads
  the file's first line — every narrator after the first was silently
  dropped for any multi-narrator book. Narrators are now joined the way
  Audiobookshelf's own parser expects, so all of them show up.
- a book's `.opf` listed narrators under `<dc:contributor opf:role="nrt">`,
  which matches the OPF spec but not what Audiobookshelf reads — its parser
  only looks at `dc:creator`. Every narrator ABM has ever written to an OPF
  file was invisible to Audiobookshelf. Narrators are now written as
  `dc:creator opf:role="nrt"`, the same element authors use.
- author and narrator names written to tags, `reader.txt`, and `.opf` files
  were joined with `; `. Audiobookshelf splits those fields on its own
  precedence — `&` first, then `and`, then `;` — so a name that itself
  contains one of those characters (an author credited as "Anne & Todd
  McCaffrey", for example) got split apart instead of read as one name.
  Names are now joined with `&` with those characters stripped from each
  individual name first, so Audiobookshelf's `&` split always wins and never
  fires in the wrong place.

  **None of the four metadata fixes above rewrite what's already on disk.** They only
  change what ABM writes from now on. If you want an existing book's tags,
  `reader.txt`, or `.opf` corrected, re-tag it or use the "Create reader.txt"
  / "Create .opf" actions to regenerate them.

### Changed

- all four `/api/metadata` endpoints that create files — `cover.jpg`,
  `reader.txt`, `desc.txt` and `.opf` — now reuse the same code library import
  and refresh already use, instead of second copies that carried the same
  metadata bugs independently. One visible
  side effect: creating an OPF for a book with no audio file on record now
  falls back to `title.opf` instead of `<Book Title>.opf`. Nothing in ABM
  reads that fallback name back, so this only matters if you were relying
  on the old filename yourself.

### Fixed

- adding chapters to a file (Chapterize, and Convert's step that embeds
  fetched chapter data into a source that had none) wiped every embedded
  global tag — title, author, narrator, ASIN, description — from the
  output. The ffmpeg command mapped metadata only from the chapters file,
  which carries chapter markers and nothing else, so the container ended
  up with none either. Convert and Merge run through the same step, but
  had it masked: a database re-tag runs after them regardless, so the
  file got its tags back anyway. Chapterize has no such re-tag step, so
  the loss was permanent — chapterizing a book actually stripped it of
  its tags, not just risked it. Fixed by keeping the source's own global
  tags and layering the chapter markers on top instead of replacing
  everything. **If you've chapterized a book, or converted one that
  picked up chapters this way, before this fix:** its embedded tags are
  still gone and this fix won't bring them back — re-tag the file with an
  external tool or replace it from wherever it originally came from.
- the same metadata-wiping command ran on the Audible download decrypt
  path too, and nothing masked it there: `write_audio_tags` defaults to
  off for Audible downloads, so no re-tag step ever ran to put the title,
  author, and ASIN back. Every Audible book decrypted before this fix is
  missing those tags in the file itself. Same fix, same caveat: already-
  decrypted files won't recover on their own.
- adding chapters to a file in place could delete the very file it had
  just finished producing. The temp file ffmpeg wrote to and the final
  destination were tracked under the same variable once the move to its
  final location succeeded, so the cleanup step that's supposed to remove
  the temp file removed the finished file instead — silently, right after
  reporting success. This hit the same three operations as above:
  Chapterize (single file and multi-file), and Convert's post-conversion
  chapter-embed step.

### Fixed

- the Library Import results screen never showed a publication year, for
  any folder, anywhere on the page. The frontend was reading a `year` field
  the backend has never sent — the parser emits `release_year` — so both
  the manual-search dropdown and the "Matched Audiobook" column came up
  blank. It was broken on the backend side too, independently: that column
  is populated automatically for every scanned folder as soon as the page
  loads, and none of the three ways a match gets built for it — ASIN,
  title search, series search — was copying `release_year` into the match
  data at all. Both are fixed.
- a folder matched by ASIN never got cover art on the Library Import
  results screen. That lookup used Libex's raw response directly instead
  of parsing it first, so the cover image field came back empty every
  time; title-search and series-search matches were unaffected. It's now
  parsed the same way manual search already did.

### Added

- the Audible Library page can now show Virtual Voice and Subscription Plans
  icons on its books, matching Library and Discover. It could already sort
  and filter by that data, but the options modal had no toggle to display
  it, so there was no way to see it even if you owned the titles. Both are
  off by default, the same as on Library and Discover.

### Changed

- Libex's metadata host is moving off `libex.lostcartographer.xyz` ahead of
  that host's retirement; ABM now points at `libexdb.com` by default. **If
  you had the `LIBEX_BASE_URL` environment variable set to override it:**
  that variable is gone and no longer has any effect — ABM always uses
  `libexdb.com` now.
- the "Release Date" column and toggle on Library, Series, and Audible
  Library only ever showed a year, never a full date. Relabeled to "Release
  Year" so the label matches what's actually shown.

### Fixed

- System > Status always showed the database as "PostgreSQL (connected)"
  under Database, no matter what was actually running or whether it could be
  reached — the row was never checked, just always displayed that way. It now
  opens the database and reports what's really there, e.g. "SQLite 3.45.1",
  and if the database can't be reached it says "unavailable" instead of
  claiming it's connected.
- interactive indexer search (the search dialog on the book detail page) no
  longer waits for indexers one at a time. Indexers within a tier are now
  queried at once instead of in sequence, so the wait is roughly the
  slowest indexer's response time rather than the sum of every enabled
  indexer's. A slow or failing indexer no longer holds up the rest —
  concurrency is capped at 5 at once, so a setup with several indexers
  behind the same proxy isn't hit with a bigger burst than that.
- "Add Series" could report success after adding only the first book. It
  created that book, then waited a fixed amount of time hoping the rest of
  the series had finished being set up before checking once — on a slower
  server, a large series, or a busy machine, that single check could land
  too early. When it did, the rest of the books were silently skipped, but
  the app still showed the add as successful and closed the dialog. It now
  keeps checking until the series is actually ready, for up to 10 seconds,
  before adding the rest.
- "Add Series" now tells you when it fails instead of closing the dialog
  regardless. The dialog stays open while the series is being added, and if
  something goes wrong — most commonly a slow catalog build that hadn't
  finished in time — it stays open with a message explaining what happened,
  and the buttons re-enable so you can just try again. When the failure
  happened after a log was already being written for the attempt, the
  message includes a "View Related Logs" link straight to it; if nothing had
  gotten far enough to produce a log, there's no link.
- the Virtual Voice and subscription-plan icons on Library, Discover, and
  Audible Library announced nothing to a screen reader — they were silently
  skipped over, so anyone relying on one had no way to know a book was
  AI-narrated or included with a subscription. They now announce as
  "AI-narrated (Audible Virtual Voice)" and "Included with Audible
  subscription plans: <plan names>". This has been broken since these icons
  were introduced, not just on the new Audible Library toggle above.
- Virtual Voice sorting and filtering on the Audible Library page could give
  the wrong answer for any book that was already in your library before that
  data started being tracked — it had been permanently recorded as
  AI-narrated whether or not it actually was, so filtering for
  non-Virtual-Voice titles could turn up nothing even though you own plenty.
  A normal library sync already corrects a book the next time it runs, but
  anything that hadn't been re-synced since was still wrong. This is
  repaired for every remaining case automatically as part of upgrading, so
  the new toggle above shows the right icon for everyone from the start.
- an Audible-library sync that fell back to the Audible API instead of
  Libex — which happens whenever Libex can't be reached — could silently
  blank out a book's series, genres, release date, rating, Virtual Voice
  status, subscription plans, and Audible ownership type. The fallback
  builder asserted a default for every field it had no data for, and a sync
  writes every field it builds, so a prior Libex sync's real values got
  overwritten with those defaults. This is now closed for every field on
  that path: the fallback builder leaves a field alone instead of guessing
  at it when it has nothing to say, and extracts series and release date
  from the Audible payload where that payload does carry them. If your
  library synced while Libex was unreachable before this fix, the affected
  books won't recover on their own — a normal sync refills them from Libex
  the next time it runs; trigger one manually if you don't want to wait for
  the schedule.
- a book's release date could show as a day earlier than it actually is.
  Upstream sends a release date as a full timestamp even though it carries
  no time of day, and stored that way it reads as a UTC instant — any
  client behind UTC renders the day before. This came in through more than
  one path: normal metadata syncing, adding a book manually with a release
  date supplied directly, and the Audible fallback used when Libex has no
  date for the ASIN. Release dates are now stored and validated as a plain
  calendar date everywhere they're written, with an invalid one rejected
  rather than stored, and any date already stored as a full timestamp is
  corrected automatically as part of upgrading.
- the library-import manual-search and preview API endpoints
  (`/api/library-import/search`, `/api/library-import/preview/{asin}`) handed
  the raw Libex response straight to the response formatter instead of
  parsing it first. A direct ASIN search or preview came back with no cover,
  no release date, and no runtime; every search — ASIN, title, author, or
  series alike — came back with no publication year and no subtitle, because
  the formatter was reading those two under names the parser has never used.
  Both are corrected. Neither endpoint has a caller anywhere in ABM today —
  not the frontend, not any background handler — so this is a fix to the
  public API contract those endpoints advertise, not something you'll see
  change on screen.
- the Audible Library page's release year could come out a year off for a
  book near a year boundary. Its release date was sent to the browser as a
  full UTC-tagged instant even though it's only ever a calendar date, so a
  browser behind UTC could compute the wrong year from it — the year shown
  on poster and overview cards, and sorting by year, were both affected.
  Year is now read off the bare calendar date instead.
- the Audible Library page showed a book as unmonitored, even when it
  wasn't, whenever it matched your library by ASIN rather than through its
  stored link — that code path resolved the match but never read the
  matched book's monitored flag. Fixed. Loading the page is also faster
  with a large Audible library: each book's library match is now looked up
  in one batched query instead of one query per book, and the page no
  longer writes to the database as a side effect of loading it.
- a saved filter created on the Library, Series, or Discover page showed up
  — and could be applied — on all three, because the three pages shared one
  stored-filters slot. Each page now keeps its own. **If you have saved
  filters:** they were stored under the old shared slot, which nothing
  reads anymore, so they won't appear after upgrading — recreate the ones
  you want to keep on each page.
